title: Revenue, Receivables & Cash Flow Review
description: Integrate revenue recognition, receivables, credit losses, cash collections, and cash flow effects.
html:
Connecting Revenue, Receivables, and Cash

Revenue recognition, accounts receivable, credit losses, and cash collections are closely connected, but they do not necessarily occur at the same time.

REVENUE RECOGNITION ≠ CASH COLLECTION

A company may recognize revenue before cash is collected, at the same time cash is collected, or after cash was collected in advance.

The Revenue Recognition Model

For revenue from contracts with customers, ASC 606 uses a five-step model.

STEP 1 IDENTIFY THE CONTRACT STEP 2 IDENTIFY THE PERFORMANCE OBLIGATIONS STEP 3 DETERMINE THE TRANSACTION PRICE STEP 4 ALLOCATE THE TRANSACTION PRICE STEP 5 RECOGNIZE REVENUE WHEN (OR AS) PERFORMANCE OBLIGATIONS ARE SATISFIED

Revenue Before Cash Collection

Assume a company provides $40,000 of services on account and has satisfied its performance obligation.

Accounts Receivable + $40,000
Revenue + $40,000
Cash No Immediate Effect
Net Income + $40,000

Revenue recognition increased income even though no cash was collected at that time.

Later Collection of the Receivable

If the customer later pays the $40,000:

Cash + $40,000
Accounts Receivable − $40,000
Revenue No New Revenue
Net Income No Effect

Collecting an existing receivable does not create revenue again.

Cash Collected Before Revenue

If cash is collected before the company satisfies the related performance obligation, the company generally records a contract liability.

CASH RECEIVED BEFORE PERFORMANCE → CONTRACT LIABILITY

When the performance obligation is later satisfied:

REDUCE CONTRACT LIABILITY + RECOGNIZE REVENUE

Example — Advance Payment

A customer pays $60,000 in advance. At year-end, the company has satisfied 40% of the related performance obligation.

REVENUE RECOGNIZED = $60,000 × 40% = $24,000 CONTRACT LIABILITY REMAINING = $60,000 − $24,000 = $36,000

Accounts Receivable and Credit Losses

Recording a receivable does not mean the company expects to collect every dollar.

The allowance for credit losses reduces gross accounts receivable to the amount expected to be collected.

NET ACCOUNTS RECEIVABLE = GROSS ACCOUNTS RECEIVABLE − ALLOWANCE FOR CREDIT LOSSES

Example — Required Allowance

Gross accounts receivable are $500,000.

The required ending allowance for credit losses is $30,000.

$500,000 − $30,000 = $470,000 NET ACCOUNTS RECEIVABLE

Adjusting the Allowance

FAR may give you an existing balance in the allowance account and ask for the required credit loss expense.

Required ending allowance: $30,000 credit

Existing allowance balance before adjustment: $8,000 credit

REQUIRED ADJUSTMENT = $30,000 − $8,000 = $22,000

The adjustment increases credit loss expense and increases the allowance by $22,000.

Watch for a Debit Balance

Suppose instead the allowance has a $4,000 debit balance before adjustment and the required ending credit balance is $30,000.

REQUIRED ADJUSTMENT = $30,000 + $4,000 = $34,000

A pre-adjustment debit balance means the adjustment must first eliminate that debit and then establish the required credit balance.

Writing Off a Specific Account

Under the allowance method, writing off a specific uncollectible receivable reduces both accounts receivable and the allowance.

Accounts Receivable Decrease
Allowance for Credit Losses Decrease
Net Accounts Receivable No Immediate Effect
Credit Loss Expense No New Expense

This is a common FAR trap. The expected loss was recognized through the allowance process, not when the specific account was later written off.

Revenue and the Statement of Cash Flows

Under the indirect method, the operating section begins with net income and adjusts for differences between accrual accounting and operating cash flows.

INCREASE IN ACCOUNTS RECEIVABLE → SUBTRACT FROM NET INCOME DECREASE IN ACCOUNTS RECEIVABLE → ADD TO NET INCOME

Why?

An increase in accounts receivable generally means revenue recognized exceeded cash collected from customers.

Net income: $200,000

Accounts receivable increased: $25,000

$200,000 − $25,000 = $175,000 BEFORE CONSIDERING OTHER OPERATING ADJUSTMENTS

Contract Liabilities and Operating Cash Flow

An increase in a contract liability can occur when cash has been collected before the related revenue is recognized.

Under the indirect method, an increase in an operating liability is generally added to net income when reconciling to operating cash flow.

Receivables Turnover

RECEIVABLES TURNOVER = NET CREDIT SALES ÷ AVERAGE NET ACCOUNTS RECEIVABLE

A higher turnover generally indicates that receivables are being collected more quickly, although interpretation should consider the company's business and credit policies.

Average Collection Period

AVERAGE COLLECTION PERIOD ≈ 365 ÷ RECEIVABLES TURNOVER

Integrated Example

A company reports:

Beginning accounts receivable: $80,000

Ending accounts receivable: $110,000

Revenue on account: $500,000

Ignore write-offs and other adjustments.

The increase in receivables is:

$110,000 − $80,000 = $30,000

Therefore, cash collected from customers is:

$500,000 − $30,000 = $470,000

FAR Problem-Solving Strategy

ASK THREE QUESTIONS: 1. WHEN WAS REVENUE EARNED? 2. WHEN WAS CASH COLLECTED? 3. WHAT HAPPENED TO THE RELATED RECEIVABLE OR LIABILITY?

Separating those three events prevents many revenue and cash-flow mistakes.

Key Takeaways

  • Revenue recognition and cash collection can occur at different times.
  • Collecting an existing receivable does not create additional revenue.
  • Cash collected before performance generally creates a contract liability.
  • Net receivables equal gross receivables less the allowance for credit losses.
  • A write-off under the allowance method does not immediately change net receivables or create new credit loss expense.
  • Under the indirect cash-flow method, increases in operating receivables generally reduce operating cash flow relative to net income.

quiz.prompt: A company's accounts receivable increased by $30,000 during the year. The company reported $500,000 of revenue on account. Ignoring write-offs and other adjustments, how much cash was collected from customers?
quiz.explanation: Accounts receivable increased because revenue on account exceeded cash collections. Cash collected equals $500,000 of revenue on account minus the $30,000 increase in accounts receivable, or $470,000.
